title: Foreword
text: The Foreword, written by the Ahl al-Bayt World Assembly (ABWA), frames the book as part of a broader project defending the sanctity of the Islamic message. It states that the arguments of scholars belonging to the School of the Ahl al-Bayt are based on genuine scholarship and appeal to reason, avoiding prejudice and bias. The Assembly expresses gratitude to the author, Professor Murtada Mutahhari, and the translator, Mrs. Zaynab Muhammadi 'Iraqi.

title: Introduction — The problem of dissimilar Imam methodologies
text: Mutahhari opens by posing the central problem of the book: Imam al-Husayn's approach (open revolt against Yazid) appears to contradict the approach of the other Imams, including 'Ali, al-Hassan, al-Sajjad and al-Sadiq, all of whom practiced taqiyyah (dissimulation) at various points. If dissimulation was religiously justified, why did al-Husayn not use it despite having the grounds to do so? If it was not justified, why did the other Imams use it and command their followers to do so? This is a fundamental debate regardless of whether the Imams' methodologies were similar or different.

title: Introduction — Taqiyyah and the richness/danger of having many Imams
text: Taqiyyah (dissimulation, hiding one's beliefs under pressure) is closely associated with Shi'ism. Because the Shi'ah accept the sayings and deeds of fourteen infallibles as testament (more numerous even than the hadiths in the Sunni Sihah al-Sittah — Al-Kafi alone reportedly contains more than 16,000 hadiths), Shi'ism has never needed qiyas (analogical reasoning) or istihsan (juristic preference). But this richness is also a danger: fourteen leaders announcing different routes and traditions, without careful research, can be exploited by those who wish to use religion for their own immoral aims, producing chaos, dispersal and a lack of morals — 'once a patient has too many doctors, there is no hope for recovery.'

title: Introduction — Imam al-Sadiq and the wealthy man's house
text: Apparent contradictions between the Imams' lifestyles (the Prophet and 'Ali living in poverty and patched clothing vs. Imam al-Hassan, al-Sadiq and al-Rida living well) are resolved by recognizing that religion adapts its expression to the exigencies of time, while its essence (sympathy, compassion, equality, justice, fairness) stays constant. Imam al-Sadiq once visited a wealthy man living in a small house who explained he kept his late father's house; the Imam replied: 'If your father was lacking common sense, does that mean you should be foolish like he was?' — establishing that inherited custom is not itself a religious value.

title: Introduction — Sufyan al-Thawri's objection to Imam al-Sadiq's fine clothing
text: Sufyan al-Thawri objected to Imam al-Sadiq wearing fine clothing, since the Prophet did not. The Imam replied that the Prophet lived a middle-class lifestyle appropriate to his own time and that Islam does not command any particular manner of dress; it commands sympathy, compassion, equality, justice and fairness. 'As you see me now, I am aware of the responsibilities towards my possessions, thus there is no logical or spiritual difference between my method and the Prophet's.' During a famine in Imam al-Sadiq's time, he ordered his stocked wheat sold in the market and bought ordinary market bread (mixed oat and wheat) for his own household, illustrating fairness over ritualized asceticism.

title: Introduction — 'Ali and the tradition on dyeing the beard
text: A second example: 'Ali used to narrate the hadith 'Color the white hairs in the beard and do not let yourselves resemble the Jews' but never acted upon it himself. He explained that the order was a wartime tactic specific to the Prophet's time (so the enemy could not distinguish old soldiers from young in the army), not a permanent religious commandment. Mutahhari uses this and the Imam al-Sadiq clothing example to introduce the interpretive method of 'conventional reconciliation' (al-jam' al-'urfi) — resolving apparent contradictions between the Imams' practices by attending to the necessities of their respective times, rather than assuming a fixed literal command binding for all eras.

title: Ch1 — 'Ali's reluctance to accept the caliphate
text: 'Ali initially refused the caliphate after 'Uthman's assassination despite people insisting on swearing allegiance to him, saying (Nahj al-Balaghah, Sermon 91): 'Leave me and seek someone else. We are facing a matter that has several sides and colors, which neither hearts can bear nor intelligence fathom... You should know that if I respond to you, I will lead you as I know how (not how you want me to)... At present, I would rather stay a minister than to become a chief.' Mutahhari reads this as 'Ali foreseeing the immense problems that would in fact later materialize during his caliphate.

title: Ch1 — 'Uthman's assassination and the problem of hypocrisy
text: 'Ali inherited a caliphate poisoned by 'Uthman's assassination. 'Ali had acted as mediator between 'Uthman and the revolutionaries, disagreeing with 'Uthman's favoritism toward relatives but also opposing 'opening the door' to killing a caliph. Mu'awiyah covertly worked to escalate the unrest that led to 'Uthman's murder, then exploited it for his own political advantage — sending 'Uthman's blood-stained shirt and his wife's severed fingers to Damascus, hanging them up, and inciting the people to avenge 'Uthman's blood against 'Ali. Unlike the Prophet's opponents (open polytheists under the slogan 'Long Live Hubal'), 'Ali faced an intelligent, non-religious group that pretended to follow Islam while pursuing anti-Islamic aims — using Qur'an 17:33 ('whosoever is killed unjustly, we have given his heir authority') as a deceptive slogan despite Mu'awiyah having no real kinship claim to 'Uthman's blood. This led directly to the battles of Jamal and Siffin.

title: Ch1 — Inflexibility in justice and bluntness in politics
text: 'Ali refused to allocate special subsidies to influential people (a custom that had crept in after the Prophet's death), saying: 'Are you asking me to gain victory and success in politics at the price of oppression and destroying the rights of powerless people?! I swear upon the Almighty, as long as there is day and night in this world, I will not do such a thing.' His bluntness and honesty in politics also drew criticism from his own supporters, who argued 'some dishonesty and deception is necessary' in politics and unfavorably compared him to the more 'tactful' Mu'awiyah. 'Ali responded (Sermon 199) that Mu'awiyah is not more cunning than him — 'he is deceitful... If Allah did not consider deception as his enemy, you would have seen that 'Ali would have been the most cunning of all people' — but that such deceitfulness is immoral, evil, wicked and blasphemous.

title: Ch1 — Why the Kharijites were 'Ali's fundamental problem: the Prophet's 13-year training period vs. 'Ali's untrained converts
text: Mutahhari explains the structural cause of the Kharijite problem. During his 13 years in Mecca, the Prophet trained a small, deeply grounded core group before any war was permitted — even under torture, he refused permission for jihad, consenting only to emigration. This created a group (~1,000 by the time of migration) who deeply understood Islam's essence, not just its outward form. Under the later caliphs, especially 'Uthman's, this training method was neglected in favor of rapid conquest, producing a new class of Muslims familiar only with Islam's outward 'crust' — exemplified by people with calloused foreheads from excessive prostration, described by Ibn 'Abbas after visiting the future rebels: 'Their foreheads are wounded because of excessive prostrations; they have hands that have calluses like the knee of a camel... Most manifest are their resolute and indomitable faces.' 'Ali described this class bluntly: 'They are a people who are rough, remorseless, tough, hard-hearted, rude, but with inferior, slavish characters and spirits... They do not know what the Qur'an is. They do not understand the meaning of the Qur'an.'

title: Ch1 — The Qur'ans-on-spears stratagem at Siffin
text: At Siffin, when Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As realized they were losing, they ordered Qur'ans raised on spear-points, provoking the untrained pietist faction within 'Ali's own army to refuse to keep fighting ('We shall not fight the Qur'an'). 'Ali objected: 'They have not brought forward the Qur'an itself but its papers and cover so that they can rise up again against this very Qur'an... I am your imam. I am your speaking Qur'an.' The faction accused 'Ali of having his own ambitions and refused to continue. When Malik al-Ashtar was on the verge of victory, they threatened to kill 'Ali himself unless Malik was recalled (they numbered about 20,000); 'Ali sent word for Malik to return.

title: Ch1 — Arbitration, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and the birth of Kharijite doctrine
text: The faction insisted on arbitration and rejected 'Ali's proposed arbitrators (Ibn 'Abbas, then Malik al-Ashtar), instead forcing Abu Musa al-Ash'ari on him — a former governor 'Ali had removed, and 'in his heart an enemy of 'Ali.' Abu Musa was outmaneuvered by 'Amr ibn al-'As in the arbitration. Realizing they had been tricked, the faction did not conclude that they erred in halting the fight or in choosing Abu Musa; instead they declared that appointing any human arbitrator was itself blasphemy, citing Qur'an 6:57 ('The judgment belongs to none but Allah'), and demanded 'Ali repent alongside them for having become 'a non-believer like us.' 'Ali refused: 'Arbitration is no blasphemy. You do not understand the meaning of the verse... I shall never confess to a sin I have never committed.' They split from him, forming the Kharijite sect ('the rebels against 'Ali').

title: Ch1 — 'Ali's tolerance of the Kharijites before their armed revolt
text: 'Ali tolerated the Kharijites' open disrespect for a long period before they turned to armed insurrection: he never cut their share of the treasury or restricted their freedom. When a Kharijite in the crowd cursed him after a masterful answer to a question ('May Allah kill him, how knowledgeable he is'), 'Ali stopped his companions from retaliating: 'Leave him be. He cursed me. The most you can do to him is to curse him. Leave him alone.' During prayer, a Kharijite named Ibn al-Kawwab repeatedly interrupted 'Ali by reciting Qur'an 39:65 (implying his deeds were nullified by 'polytheism'); 'Ali, obeying 7:204 ('when the Qur'an is recited, listen and keep silent'), stayed silent each time, then on the third or fourth repetition recited 30:60 ('let not those who have no certitude make you unstable') and continued his prayer without further reaction.

title: Ch1 — The Kharijite sect's formal doctrines
text: The Kharijites formalized their break into a religious sect with explicit doctrines: (1) 'Uthman, 'Ali, Mu'awiyah, and all who accepted arbitration are non-believers, except those who repented; (2) 'enjoining good and forbidding evil' is obligatory and unconditional — one must rise against any unlawful or cruel ruler even believing the rising will fail; (3) faith is inseparable from action — a single major sin (lying, drinking, backbiting) expels a person from Islam entirely. The practical result: they considered themselves the only true Muslims, declared others' meat forbidden and intermarriage forbidden, and — most extremely — considered killing the women and children of non-Kharijites permissible. They killed a passing companion of the Prophet and his pregnant wife (ripping open her stomach) for refusing to disown 'Ali, and rebuked a man for eating a single date from an unattended garden as 'intruding on your Muslim brother's wealth.'

title: Ch1 — Nahrawan: negotiation, the banner, and the battle
text: When the Kharijites' actions escalated from words to violence, 'Ali confronted them at Nahrawan. Ibn 'Abbas was sent first but achieved nothing. 'Ali then spoke to them himself; of roughly 12,000, 8,000 repented under the protective banner 'Ali raised, and 4,000 refused and were killed in battle, with only about 10 survivors — including 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, 'Ali's future assassin. 'Ali's own verdict on the act (Sermon 92): 'It was I and I alone who removed the eye of this revolt. No one save me could have stopped them with his sword.' He explained that no ordinary believer would have had the nerve to draw a sword against people who appeared more pious and ascetic than himself — 'their hands would shiver, their heart would tremble' — and that only an unbeliever, acting for the wrong reasons, could otherwise have done it. He used the image of kalab (rabies): the Kharijites were like rabid dogs whose disease (fanatical false piety) would spread to whoever they bit, so that eradication, though tragic, was necessary to save the wider body of Islam from 'rigidity, petrifaction, idiocy and ignorance.'

title: Ch1 — Characteristics of the Kharijites: bravery, worship, ignorance
text: Mutahhari lists their distinguishing traits: extraordinary bravery and devotion to their cause; excessive, dogmatic worship (the source of their apparent piety and the reason no ordinary Muslim dared oppose them); and above all ignorance and lack of real Islamic knowledge, which 'Ali called their defining vice: 'You are the worst of people... because you are spears in the hands of the devil. Satan places you in his bow instead of his arrows and crushes his targets with you.' Mutahhari notes that Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As — genuine hypocrites who privately respected 'Ali (Mu'awiyah reportedly wept when 'Ali was later described to him, saying 'Time can never again bring a person like 'Ali') — deliberately used ignorant pietist factions as tools to achieve their political ends, a pattern Mutahhari says recurs 'in various guises' throughout history.

title: Ch1 — The Iqbal/Ja'far-Sadiq rumor as a modern parable of Kharijite-style ignorance
text: Mutahhari recounts a contemporary anecdote: a rumor spread that the poet Muhammad Iqbal had cursed Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq in his writing, based on a couplet actually condemning two historical traitors coincidentally also named Ja'far (of Bengal) and Sadiq (of Deccan) who betrayed Muslim rulers to British colonizers. Mutahhari traces the rumor to its source and shows it to be a complete misreading, using it as a direct parallel to Kharijite-style thinking: declaring people non-believers or heretics based on surface impressions without careful investigation. He urges: 'Investigate! Investigate... then say whatever you want, but do not say anything before you have done your research,' explicitly invoking the Nahrawan Kharijites as the cautionary example ('Do not be like the Nahrawan Kharijites').

title: Ch1 — Ibn Muljam, Qatam, and the assassination plot
text: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam was one of nine ascetic Kharijites who vowed in Mecca that 'Ali, Mu'awiyah and 'Amr ibn al-'As were the causes of all the Muslim world's strife, and drew lots to assassinate each; Ibn Muljam was assigned 'Ali. In Kufah he fell in love with a Kharijite woman, Qatam, whose father and brother 'Ali had killed at Nahrawan. She agreed to marry him only on the condition — as her fourth and final dowry demand, after money, a slave boy, and a slave girl — that he kill 'Ali: 'If you seek union with me, you must kill 'Ali. If you live, you will gain what you seek, and if you die, then nothing.' He composed verses declaring no dowry in the world was as exalted as 'Ali's blood. The date chosen was the night before the 19th of Ramadan, deliberately selected — per Ibn Abi al-Hadid — because the Kharijites believed killing 'Ali on the Night of Qadr (Laylat al-Qadr) would earn greater heavenly reward.

title: Ch1 — 'Ali's final instruction on the Kharijites and his death
text: On his deathbed, 'Ali distinguished the danger of Mu'awiyah's hypocrites from that of the Kharijites and instructed his followers: 'After me, do not kill the Kharijites anymore, because whoever seeks truth and commits a mistake is not the same as the one who seeks falsehood from the beginning and has reached it' — since killing them further would only serve Mu'awiyah's interests, not truth and justice. When Ibn Muljam was captured and brought before the dying 'Ali, 'Ali asked him, 'Why did you do such a thing? Was I a bad Imam for you?' Ibn Muljam, unrepentant, said he had vowed to kill the worst of God's creatures with that sword; 'Ali replied that his prayer had indeed been answered, since he himself would be killed by that same sword. 'Ali died on the night of the 21st of Ramadan and was buried in secret by his closest family, his grave's location concealed for about a hundred years — out of fear the Kharijites would desecrate it — until Imam al-Sadiq revealed it publicly after the Umayyad dynasty's fall.

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — Framing the question of al-Hassan's peace vs al-Husayn's revolt
text: Mutahhari opens Session 1 by posing the puzzle directly: why did Imam al-Hassan make peace with Mu'awiyah while Imam al-Husayn refused to submit to Yazid? He rejects the easy explanation that the two Imams simply had different temperaments (one peace-loving, one rebellious), arguing instead that a proper answer requires first laying out Islam's general jurisprudential rules on jihad and peace, since both men's choices were reasoned applications of those same rules to different circumstances, not personality traits.

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — The Prophet's own alternation between peace and war
text: Mutahhari shows that pacifism was not unique to al-Hassan: the Prophet himself avoided armed retaliation throughout the Meccan period even as Muslims were tortured, and permission to fight was only revealed after the migration to Medina (citing Qur'an 22:39). The Prophet later both fought polytheists, Jews and Christians at times and signed treaties with them at other times (e.g., the Hudaybiyyah treaty and a non-aggression pact with the Jews of Medina), showing that Islam treats war and peace as circumstance-dependent tools rather than fixed identities.

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — 'Ali's own record of restraint and arbitration
text: Mutahhari traces the same pattern in 'Ali: he refused to fight for the caliphate after the Prophet's death (drawing even Fatimah's objection), mediated between the rebels and 'Uthman to try to prevent his murder, and later accepted arbitration at Siffin after Mu'awiyah's side raised the Qur'an on spearheads — even though 'Amr ibn al-'As then manipulated the arbitration to a fruitless outcome. Mutahhari uses this to argue that 'Ali, like the Prophet, moved between war and peace based on the situation, which sets up the same question for al-Hassan and al-Husayn.

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — The categories of jihad in Shi'ah jurisprudence
text: Mutahhari outlines, citing the jurists Muhaqqiq al-Hilli and Shahid Thani, several distinct categories of jihad: (1) 'antecedent' offensive jihad against non-Muslims, which requires the presence of an imam or his appointee and is not permitted even to a religious authority acting alone; (2) defensive jihad when Islamic land, people, or property are attacked, which becomes obligatory on all Muslims regardless of an imam's permission, with the obligation growing stronger the closer one is to the danger; and (3) a jihad-like category (not classed as general jihad but earning the same martyrdom status) covering a Muslim in non-Muslim lands who must fight to save his own life, or someone defending his home from an attacker, where the level of resistance required scales with what is at stake (property vs. life).

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — Fighting rebels against a just ruler
text: A further category is fighting rebels: when two Muslim factions clash, the Qur'an (49:9) commands the community first to seek reconciliation, and only to fight the side that refuses to comply. Mutahhari notes this applies especially when a group rises against a just imam, in which case Muslims are obligated to fight in the imam's favor, and mentions a related but separately debated category of righteous armed uprising for 'enjoining good and forbidding evil.'

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — Jurisprudential conditions for a peace treaty (armistice)
text: Mutahhari then turns to the jurisprudence of peace/truce, quoting Muhaqqiq's Shara'i' al-Islam: a truce with non-Muslims is permissible only if it serves Muslim interests — e.g., the Muslims are currently too few or weak to win, they need time to gather strength or allies, or the pause in hostilities is likely to lead the other side toward Islam — and even then it must run for a fixed, specified term rather than an indefinite one. If Muslims are strong enough to prevail and gain nothing from a truce, a truce is not permitted; this framework is what Mutahhari will apply to evaluate al-Hassan's treaty.

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — The Hudaybiyyah precedent
text: Mutahhari retells the Hudaybiyyah episode at length as the model for al-Hassan's later peace: the Prophet marched to Mecca unarmed as a pilgrim, was blocked by the Quraysh, and accepted an apparently one-sided ten-year truce (including a clause requiring the return of any Muslim who fled to Medina, but not vice versa) purely to secure freedom to preach — a decision many companions, including 'Umar, initially resented. Within less than two years, this peace produced far more conversions than the previous two decades of conflict had, vindicating the Prophet's judgment and establishing that a costly-looking peace can be the strategically sound choice.

title: Chapter 2 Session 1 — Q&A: does citing jurisprudence beg the question, and is Sunni fiqh on jihad different?
text: In the Q&A, a listener presses Mutahhari on whether it is circular to judge al-Hassan's conduct by a jurisprudence that is itself built on the Imams' precedents; Mutahhari clarifies he is testing whether the jurisprudence as a whole is internally logical, not claiming al-Hassan consciously followed later fiqh manuals. Asked whether Sunni jurisprudence differs on jihad, he says the substantive rules are close, with Shi'ah fiqh's distinguishing feature being its requirement of an imam's authorization for offensive jihad.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — First contrast: al-Hassan held the caliphate, al-Husayn did not
text: Opening Session 2, Mutahhari lists the concrete differences between the two Imams' situations, starting with political position: al-Hassan was the sitting caliph facing a rebellion, so his death in battle would have meant the death of the established leader of the Muslims, similar in kind to 'Uthman's assassination. Al-Husayn, by contrast, held no office and was killed as a protester against an already-entrenched illegitimate government, making his death a mark of honor rather than a blow to legitimate authority.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — Second contrast: military balance and a demoralized Kufah
text: Mutahhari argues that even a large Iraqi army under al-Hassan (estimated at 30,000-100,000) would not have matched Mu'awiyah's roughly 150,000 troops, especially given that 'Ali's larger and stronger force had still failed to defeat Mu'awiyah at Siffin. Kufah itself was riddled with hypocrisy, bribery by Mu'awiyah's agents, and the aftermath of Kharijite unrest, so a war would likely have dragged on for years, cost many lives, and still ended in al-Hassan's defeat and death without any of Karbala's clarity or glory.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — Third contrast: no demand for allegiance was made of al-Hassan
text: Mutahhari identifies the first of three elements behind al-Husayn's uprising: the Umayyad regime's demand that he personally swear allegiance to Yazid, which al-Husayn flatly refused. He notes that Mu'awiyah never demanded such an oath from al-Hassan — in fact the peace treaty explicitly excluded any pledge of allegiance — so this trigger for revolt simply did not exist in al-Hassan's case.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — Fourth contrast: Kufah's invitation to al-Husayn vs its exhaustion under al-Hassan
text: The second element was Kufah's mass invitation: some eighteen thousand letters urged al-Husayn to lead an uprising, creating what Mutahhari calls an 'ultimatum' he could not ignore without being faulted by history. Under al-Hassan, conditions were the opposite — Kufah was exhausted, riddled with Kharijite hostility (he reportedly wore armor even to lead prayers after being shot at), and its people showed no readiness to fight, so no comparable invitation or obligation existed for him.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — Fifth contrast: Mu'awiyah's proven tyranny under Yazid vs. his still-unproven record under al-Hassan
text: The third element was the duty to 'enjoin good and forbid evil' against manifest, ongoing oppression: by al-Husayn's time Mu'awiyah's rule (and Yazid's dissolute succession) had two decades of documented corruption and injustice behind it. When al-Hassan negotiated, Mu'awiyah had not yet shown his true character and in fact offered a signed blank paper promising to rule by the Qur'an and the Prophet's practice — conditions that, on their face, gave al-Hassan no legitimate pretext to insist on war instead of accepting a seemingly favorable peace.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — Terms of the peace treaty
text: Mutahhari summarizes the treaty's key clauses: governance would pass to Mu'awiyah only on condition he follow the Qur'an, the Prophet's practice, and the conduct of earlier caliphs; succession after Mu'awiyah would revert to al-Hassan and then al-Husayn (i.e., the peace was explicitly temporary); Mu'awiyah had to stop the public cursing of 'Ali in Syria; treasury funds were earmarked for al-Hassan, the Shi'ah community, and the families of those killed at Siffin and Jamal; and a general amnesty guaranteed the safety of 'Ali's former supporters throughout Muslim lands. Mutahhari stresses that Mu'awiyah later broke essentially every one of these terms, which is what exposed his true character to the wider community.

title: Chapter 2 Session 2 — Q&A: would 'Ali have made peace, and did al-Husayn endorse the treaty?
text: Asked whether 'Ali would have made peace in al-Hassan's shoes, Mutahhari says yes, given identical circumstances, since 'Ali's own refusal to accept Mu'awiyah applied to being ruled by him, not to the different situation of stepping aside entirely as al-Hassan did. Asked whether al-Husayn signed or objected to the treaty, Mutahhari states there is no record of his signature (none was required) and that historically al-Husayn fully deferred to and supported his brother's decision without any recorded opposition.

title: Ch3 — Zayn al-'Abidin as champion of spirituality
text: Mutahhari presents Imam Zayn al-'Abidin ('Ali ibn al-Husayn) as a model of authentic Islamic spirituality, using the Prophet's Household as an example of belief becoming deeply embodied. His worship is described as a genuine journey of the soul toward Allah rather than merely an outward bodily act.

title: Ch3 — Absorption in worship
text: Mutahhari illustrates the Imam's intense devotion through the incident of his child suffering a broken bone while the Imam was absorbed in worship. The family treated the child without interrupting him, and the next morning he noticed the bandage and asked what had happened. The story is used to convey the depth of his spiritual concentration.

title: Ch3 — The herald of affection
text: Zayn al-'Abidin is described as a herald of affection who deliberately showed kindness to isolated people, strangers, the poor and those overlooked by society. He invited people such as lepers into his home and cared for them. Mutahhari characterizes his home as a place for the poor, orphans and helpless.

title: Ch3 — Service in the Hajj caravan
text: During Hajj, Zayn al-'Abidin preferred to travel with a caravan whose members did not know his identity, so that he could serve them without being treated as a distinguished descendant of the Prophet. When they discovered who he was, they wanted to reverse the roles, but he explained that he had deliberately chosen an unfamiliar caravan to gain the opportunity to serve Muslims and friends.

title: Ch3 — Serving Islam through another form of mission
text: Mutahhari contrasts Zayn al-'Abidin's circumstances with the opportunities given to Imam al-Husayn and Imam al-Sadiq. Although he did not rise with the sword, Mutahhari argues that service to Islam can take different forms and highlights the Imam's legacy through prayer and supplication as one such form.

title: Ch3 — Mourning Imam al-Husayn as preservation of Karbala's message
text: Mutahhari rejects the interpretation that Zayn al-'Abidin's continual mourning meant merely uncontrolled grief or that he allowed Karbala to be forgotten. He interprets the mourning as a way of preserving the memory of Imam al-Husayn's tragedy and reminding people of why he rose and who was responsible for his death. The Imam's comparison with Ya'qub's grief for Yusuf is used to explain the depth of his sorrow after witnessing the deaths of members of his family.

title: Ch4 — Why Imam al-Sadiq declined the political opening
text: The end of Umayyad rule created a major political opening because opposition had accumulated among Arabs and Persians through religious discontent, oppression, and the memory of Alawid uprisings. Mutahhari's central question is why Imam al-Sadiq did not seize this opportunity.

title: Ch4 — Abbasid secret organization and the use of Islamic slogans
text: The Abbasids exploited anti-Umayyad discontent through a secret, organized missionary network, especially in Khorasan. Their public slogans invoked the Household of the Prophet and Qur'anic ideas rather than an explicit Abbasid succession claim, allowing them to mobilize broad support.

title: Ch4 — Abu Muslim and Abu Salmah
text: The Abbasid movement relied especially on Abu Muslim in Khorasan and Abu Salmah Khallal in Kufah. Mutahhari distinguishes political effectiveness from moral character and describes the two as important operators within the movement.

title: Ch4 — Abu Salmah's double letter
text: Near the transition to Abbasid rule, Abu Salmah secretly sent essentially the same offer to Imam al-Sadiq and 'Abd Allah al-Mahd, offering to redirect the caliphate toward the family of Abu Talib. The parallel letters reveal the political nature of the proposal.

title: Ch4 — Imam al-Sadiq burns Abu Salmah's letter
text: Imam al-Sadiq did not even read Abu Salmah's letter; he burned it and sent back a poem illustrating the danger of someone doing the work while another person reaps its outcome. Mutahhari interprets this as evidence that Abu Salmah was not acting as the Imam's sincere follower.

title: Ch4 — Imam al-Sadiq and 'Abd Allah al-Mahd
text: 'Abd Allah al-Mahd was enthusiastic about Abu Salmah's offer. Imam al-Sadiq challenged the claim that Khorasanis were his followers and warned that the proposed political venture lacked the necessary real conditions.

title: Ch4 — The Abwa' gathering and Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah
text: Before the Abbasid victory, leaders of Banu Hashim gathered at Abwa'. Muhammad, son of 'Abd Allah al-Mahd, was presented as a potential leader against the Umayyads and was associated by some with the promised Mahdi because of his name and other coincidental features.

title: Ch4 — Mahdism versus enjoining good and forbidding evil
text: When asked to pledge allegiance to Muhammad as the promised Mahdi, Imam al-Sadiq refused the Mahdi claim but stated that he would pledge support if the movement were genuinely undertaken under the principle of enjoining good and forbidding evil and fighting oppression. This distinction is central to his political stance.

title: Ch4 — Imam al-Sadiq's foresight concerning the Abbasids
text: Mutahhari presents Imam al-Sadiq as recognizing that the Abbasid political actors had their own ambitions and that Muhammad Nafs al-Zakiyyah would be killed rather than become caliph. The later historical outcome is presented as confirmation within the narrative.

title: Ch5 — Martyrdom as a shared pattern among the Imams
text: Mutahhari opens by stressing that, in his account, the infallible Imams other than the living Imam of the Time all died as martyrs. He argues that their methods should not be contrasted as though Imam al-Husayn alone resisted oppression while the others accepted it: the objective was resistance to oppressive rule, while the form of combat changed according to circumstances. It could be open warfare, condemnation and social resistance, or covert action under taqiyyah.

title: Ch5 — Imam Musa al-Kazim's imprisonment and refusal to submit
text: According to the text's account, Imam Musa al-Kazim spent about four years imprisoned and was moved among several prisons. Offers were repeatedly made that he could gain freedom by apologizing, confessing wrongdoing, or otherwise submitting to Harun. He refused these proposals. Mutahhari presents this refusal as an expression of the Imam's resistance and fidelity to his principles.

title: Ch5 — Basrah prison: 'Isa ibn Ja'far's change of view
text: The Imam was first held in Basrah under 'Isa ibn Ja'far. Although 'Isa initially accepted the government's portrayal of Musa al-Kazim as a political threat, personal contact changed his view: he came to see the Imam as a spiritual man and treated him well. When Harun secretly ordered him to get rid of the Imam, 'Isa refused and asked that the Imam be transferred rather than killed.

title: Ch5 — Baghdad prisons and the failure of Harun's pressure
text: In Baghdad the Imam was successively placed with Fadl ibn Rabi' and Fadl ibn Yahya al-Barmaki. Each, according to the narrative, became impressed by him and improved his conditions, effectively treating him more like an honored guest than a prisoner. Harun responded by transferring the Imam again and punishing or disfavoring those who treated him sympathetically, eventually placing him with Sindi ibn Shahik, where the conditions became harsh.

title: Ch5 — Harun's demand for a confession and the Imam's final refusal
text: Near the end of the imprisonment, Harun sent an intermediary with a private offer: if the Imam would simply confess wrongdoing and ask the caliph's forgiveness, he would be released. The text presents this as a test of whether the Imam would legitimize the ruler by an act of submission. Musa al-Kazim refused, indicating that his life was already nearing its end. The narrative then states that he was poisoned about a week later.

title: Ch5 — Why Harun regarded Imam al-Kazim as a threat
text: Mutahhari argues that Harun's fear was not based on an overt military uprising by the Imam. Rather, Harun perceived the Imam's spiritual authority and popularity as a rival source of legitimacy, especially while arranging allegiance to his sons as future rulers. The Imam's lineage, piety and influence could draw people's attention away from the caliphate. The text therefore describes a 'spiritual revolution' as the deeper threat perceived by Harun.

title: Ch5 — Ma'mun's account of Harun's respect and political fear
text: The chapter recounts a report attributed to Ma'mun in which Harun showed striking respect toward Musa ibn Ja'far during Hajj, welcomed him while remaining seated on horseback, asked about his family and financial circumstances, and arranged for him to be escorted out. In the account, Harun later explains that the Ahl al-Bayt were political rivals: if their material resources became strong, their supporters could potentially rally around them. Mutahhari uses this story to illustrate the tension between Harun's personal recognition of the Imam's stature and his political fear of that influence.

title: Ch5 — Spiritual influence as a form of propagation
text: Mutahhari emphasizes that the Imam's influence did not depend on armies or formal propaganda. People who encountered his worship, generosity and character could be transformed by that example. The chapter illustrates this with reports involving 'Ali ibn Yaqtin, an undercover Shi'ah official in Harun's government, and an Ahwazi believer whose heavy tax burden was resolved after the Imam sent a private letter to the governor. The broader lesson in the text is that action and character can propagate religious truth more powerfully than words alone.

title: Ch5 — Worship and care for the vulnerable as recurring Imam traditions
text: Mutahhari identifies two recurring characteristics among the Imams: profound worship, fear of Allah and monotheistic consciousness; and personal sympathy with the weak, oppressed, dispossessed and needy. He presents these not as abstract ideals but as habits repeatedly visible in the lives of the Imams. For Musa al-Kazim, the chapter connects intense worship with the prison setting and connects religious leadership with direct concern for believers in difficulty.

title: Ch5 — Bishr Hafi: the Imam's indirect reform through a single question
text: The story of Bishr Hafi illustrates the Imam's ability to reform without coercion. Passing a house where music, dancing and gambling were taking place, Musa al-Kazim asked a servant whether the house belonged to a free man or a slave. The Imam's point was that someone enslaved to Allah would not behave in such a way. Bishr understood the message, sought the Imam, and declared that from that moment he wanted to become Allah's servant. Mutahhari uses the episode as another example of spiritual influence through character and concise guidance.

title: Ch5 — Safwan Jammal and complicity with an oppressor
text: Safwan Jammal, a companion of the Imam who rented camels, had contracted to provide transportation for Harun's pilgrimage. Musa al-Kazim challenged him about whether he inwardly wished Harun to remain alive long enough to complete the journey and pay the remaining rent. When Safwan admitted that he did, the Imam taught that being content with an oppressor's survival for one's own material interest was itself morally problematic. Safwan then sold his camels and ended that business relationship. Harun discovered the reason and treated the Imam's influence as a serious threat.

title: Ch5 — Harun's attempts to break the Imam's resistance
text: The chapter gives several examples of attempts to soften or compromise the Imam: promises of release, better accommodation, special food and private assurances that the caliph did not personally regard him as sinful. The Imam repeatedly refused to become dependent on Harun or to validate his authority through apology. One episode has the Imam repeatedly beginning another prayer rather than giving Fadl ibn Rabi' an opportunity to deliver Harun's message, illustrating deliberate refusal to engage with the proposed terms.

title: Ch5 — The reported method of Imam al-Kazim's martyrdom
text: The final section reports that the Imam was held by Sindi ibn Shahik and that a poisoned preparation was administered to him. According to the narrative, officials then assembled respected people and attempted to demonstrate publicly that he was healthy and had not been harmed. The Imam contradicted this claim, saying that he had been poisoned and had only a short time left. After his death, the authorities reportedly displayed his body by the Baghdad bridge for several days and claimed that he had died naturally.

title: Ch5 — Mutahhari's three-part explanation of the martyrdom
text: At the conclusion, Mutahhari summarizes three factors behind the martyrdom: first, the Imam's very presence and spiritual authority threatened the ruling caliphs; second, the Imams opposed and exposed oppression while practicing taqiyyah so that they did not unnecessarily leave evidence that could be exploited against them; and third, the Imams possessed an exceptional spirit of resistance and could not be induced to surrender or become obedient followers of the ruler. The chapter's central logic is therefore: different historical forms of resistance do not imply acceptance of oppression.

title: Ch6 S1 — The historical problem of al-Rida as crown prince
text: The chapter examines why Imam al-Rida accepted the position of successor under Ma'mun even though the Abbasids had a long record of conflict with the Alawis. Mutahhari frames this as a historical problem comparable to Imam al-Hassan's peace: in both cases critics can argue that accepting an arrangement with an existing caliph amounted to compromise, while the Imam's defenders must explain the circumstances.

title: Ch6 S1 — Abbasid hostility toward the Alawis
text: Mutahhari describes sustained Abbasid persecution of the Alawis, including imprisonment and killing under Mansur and later rulers. He uses the treatment of their own rivals and even members of the Abbasid dynasty to establish that political power in this period was marked by severe internal rivalry as well as conflict with the Alawis.

title: Ch6 S1 — The historical sources for the succession episode
text: Mutahhari says the account should not be reconstructed solely from Shi'ah sources. He compares reports in Shaykh Mufid's al-Irshad and Shaykh Saduq's 'Uyun al-Akhbar al-Rida with Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani's Maqatil al-Talibiyyin, which he identifies as a non-Shi'ah historical source. He argues that important details in these traditions substantially correspond.

title: Ch6 S1 — Was Ma'mun sincere? Competing historical possibilities
text: Mutahhari lays out several hypotheses rather than claiming certainty: Ma'mun may initially have sincerely intended to transfer authority; Fadl ibn Sahl may have initiated the policy; or Ma'mun may have adopted the proposal for political purposes from the beginning. The chapter explicitly says historical evidence does not establish one explanation with absolute certainty.

title: Ch6 S1 — Ma'mun's reported Shi'ah sympathies versus political conduct
text: The chapter presents reports of Ma'mun's intellectual interest in Shi'ism and his respect for the Ahl al-Bayt, alongside his father's harsh treatment of Imam Musa al-Kazim and Ma'mun's own political behavior. Mutahhari uses this tension to caution against treating intellectual sympathy or personal admiration as equivalent to political loyalty.

title: Ch6 S1 — The oath Ma'mun said he made during his struggle with Amin
text: One historical explanation accepted by Shaykh Saduq and others is that Ma'mun, fearing defeat by his brother Amin, performed purification, prayer and Qur'anic recitation and vowed that if Allah gave him victory he would return the caliphate to its rightful owners. After his victories, he presented the appointment of Imam al-Rida as fulfillment of that oath. Mutahhari presents this as one probability, not as settled fact.

title: Ch6 S1 — Fadl ibn Sahl as an alternative initiator
text: Another hypothesis is that Fadl ibn Sahl, Ma'mun's powerful minister, proposed bringing Imam al-Rida into the succession. Mutahhari questions explanations that portray Fadl simply as a sincere Shi'ah supporter, noting reports that Imam al-Rida himself distrusted Fadl and warned Ma'mun about him. The chapter leaves Fadl's exact motivation unresolved.

title: Ch6 S1 — Political theory: attracting Iranian support
text: One proposed political explanation is that Ma'mun wanted to attract Iranian support by associating his government with the Alawis. Mutahhari notes the symbolic importance of the title 'al-Rida' and suggests that presenting the Imam as successor could make it appear that long-standing Iranian sympathy for the family of the Prophet had finally been accommodated.

title: Ch6 S1 — Political theory: neutralizing Alawi rebellions
text: A second political explanation is that placing Imam al-Rida inside the government could weaken recurring Alawi uprisings. If the most prominent Alawi were publicly incorporated into the succession, other rebels could lose a powerful argument that the Alawis were excluded from government. Mutahhari presents this as a hypothesis about Ma'mun's political calculation.

title: Ch6 S1 — Political theory: disarming Imam al-Rida's opposition
text: A third proposed motive is to neutralize the Imam himself by giving him a government position. Critics could then say that the Alawi claim to justice changed once its representatives received office. Mutahhari describes the general political principle as giving an opponent a position so that his opposition becomes harder to mobilize.

title: Ch6 S1 — The journey from Medina to Marw
text: The chapter identifies the forced summons of Imam al-Rida from Medina to Marw as a significant historical fact. He was brought with relatives under surveillance, and the route was deliberately selected through Basrah and Khuzistan toward Nishapur rather than through Kufah, where he might encounter Shi'ah supporters. Mutahhari emphasizes that the journey was organized without prior consultation with the Imam.

title: Ch6 S1 — The Imam's initial refusal
text: According to the historical reports discussed, Imam al-Rida rejected the proposal when it was presented in Marw. Fadl ibn Sahl and al-Hasan ibn Sahl reportedly warned that refusal meant execution; even after the threat was made explicit, the Imam continued to refuse until Ma'mun personally threatened his life.

title: Ch6 S1 — Acceptance under threat
text: Mutahhari interprets the eventual acceptance as compelled by a threat to the Imam's life. He compares Ma'mun's argument invoking Imam 'Ali's participation in the earlier council with the historical question of whether the Imam was voluntarily accepting the office or submitting to circumstances. This is presented as an important distinction for understanding the event.

title: Ch6 S1 — Imam al-Rida's condition of non-interference
text: The Imam agreed on the explicit condition that he would not interfere in government affairs or assume responsibility for Ma'mun's actions. This preserved a distinction between accepting the title and cooperating with the government. Mutahhari notes that the Imam continued to maintain distance from governmental responsibilities, including initially declining to lead the 'Id prayer.

title: Ch6 S1 — The 'Id prayer episode
text: When Ma'mun later insisted that Imam al-Rida lead the 'Id prayer, the Imam initially objected that this violated the condition of non-involvement. He eventually agreed but proceeded in a manner that, according to the narrative, generated such popular excitement that Ma'mun and Fadl feared a political upheaval and stopped him before he reached the destination.

title: Ch6 S1 — The acceptance ceremony and the Imam's independent stance
text: At the formal acceptance ceremony, Imam al-Rida delivered a short speech that did not flatter or thank Ma'mun in the conventional manner. Mutahhari interprets the speech as a concise declaration that accepting the position did not mean accepting Ma'mun's political legitimacy or becoming his collaborator.

title: Ch6 S2 — What is certain and what is doubtful
text: Mutahhari separates the succession episode into definite historical facts and doubtful interpretations. He treats the forced summons to Marw, the initial refusal, the threat of death, the eventual acceptance, and the condition of non-interference as firm elements; the precise motives behind Ma'mun's policy remain matters for historical analysis.

title: Ch6 S2 — The succession was initiated by Ma'mun, not Imam al-Rida
text: The chapter states that the crown-prince arrangement was not initiated by Imam al-Rida. Ma'mun's agents gathered people from Khorasan and summoned Banu Hashim from Medina before discussing the proposal with the Imam. The route was deliberately chosen to minimize contact with Shi'ah communities.

title: Ch6 S2 — Imam al-Rida's logical refusal of the caliphate offer
text: When Ma'mun reportedly proposed transferring the caliphate, Imam al-Rida answered that Ma'mun could not legitimately give away something that was either rightfully his or not rightfully his. If it was divinely legitimate, Ma'mun had no right to surrender it; if it was illegitimate, he had no right to transfer it. Mutahhari uses this reasoning to show why the Imam rejected the offer.

title: Ch6 S2 — Ma'mun combines argument with threat
text: After the Imam rejected the proposal, Ma'mun invoked Imam 'Ali's participation in the six-person council established by 'Umar and used that precedent as a justification for demanding compliance. The argument was accompanied by an explicit threat to kill Imam al-Rida. Mutahhari therefore distinguishes the rational argument Ma'mun offered from the coercive force behind the decision.

title: Ch6 S2 — The non-interference condition
text: Imam al-Rida accepted the crown-prince title only with the condition that he would have no practical role in government: no judgments, appointments, dismissals, administration, or other governmental duties. Mutahhari treats this condition as evidence that the Imam did not regard the appointment as ordinary political collaboration.

title: Ch6 S2 — The crown-prince speech
text: At the formal ceremony, Ma'mun arranged an elaborate public event, but Imam al-Rida's speech was extremely brief and did not praise or thank Ma'mun. Its substance, as Mutahhari interprets it, was that the Ahl al-Bayt possessed the underlying right to the caliphate and that accepting the title did not mean receiving that right from Ma'mun.

title: Ch6 S2 — The 'Id prayer demonstrates the separation
text: When Ma'mun later asked Imam al-Rida to lead the 'Id prayer, the Imam reminded him of their agreement. When he finally agreed on the condition that he would follow his grandfather's manner rather than contemporary court custom, the public response became so intense that Ma'mun ordered him brought back. Mutahhari uses this as evidence of the Imam's independent religious authority.

title: Ch6 S2 — The Fadl ibn Sahl hypothesis
text: One disputed explanation is that Fadl ibn Sahl, Ma'mun's powerful minister, initiated the crown-prince arrangement. Some historians have attributed sincere Shi'ah motives to Fadl, but Mutahhari argues that this interpretation conflicts with Imam al-Rida's own distrust of Fadl and his refusal to cooperate with him.

title: Ch6 S2 — The alternative Fadl hypothesis
text: Mutahhari considers another hypothesis: if Fadl initiated the policy, his goal may have been to use the Alawi Imam for a larger political project involving Iranian interests. He stresses that this is an assumption, not an established historical fact, and examines it as one possible explanation for the Imam's refusal to cooperate with Fadl.

title: Ch6 S2 — Baghdad's reaction to the appointment
text: When news of Imam al-Rida's appointment reached Baghdad, Abbasid leaders rejected Ma'mun's decision and pledged allegiance to another Abbasid, Ibrahim ibn Shiklah. Mutahhari uses this reaction to argue that even a successful transfer of power in Khorasan would not automatically have produced unified control over the wider Islamic territories.

title: Ch6 S2 — Ma'mun's motives remain disputed
text: If Ma'mun initiated the appointment, Mutahhari considers two broad possibilities: he may initially have had a genuine intention to transfer authority, later changing his mind; or the entire arrangement may have been a political maneuver. He reports Shaykh Saduq's account of an oath Ma'mun made during his conflict with Amin while noting that many scholars reject the idea of sincere intentions from the beginning.

title: Ch6 S2 — Possible political purpose: discrediting Imam al-Rida
text: One political interpretation is that Ma'mun wanted to draw Imam al-Rida into the governmental system so that public dissatisfaction with the government would also damage the Imam's reputation. Mutahhari describes the general political tactic as giving a respected critic an official position and then making the position fail or become unpopular.

title: Ch6 S2 — Imam al-Rida's opposition to Fadl ibn Sahl
text: The chapter reports traditions in which Fadl ibn Sahl and Hisham ibn Ibrahim approached Imam al-Rida and proposed killing Ma'mun so that the Imam could become caliph. The Imam rejected the proposal and later warned Ma'mun about them. Mutahhari presents this as evidence that the Imam did not regard Fadl's political maneuvering as trustworthy.

title: Ch6 S2 — Why acceptance could still be religiously justified
text: Mutahhari asks whether Imam al-Rida should simply have accepted death rather than the crown-prince title. He distinguishes this from Imam al-Husayn's situation: al-Husayn faced an explicit demand for allegiance to Yazid and a historical need for public awakening, whereas al-Rida faced a different choice in which accepting a formal position under coercion did not necessarily constitute the same kind of religious compromise.

title: Ch6 S2 — Cooperation with rulers: Safwan Jammal and 'Ali ibn Yaqtin
text: The chapter compares two apparently opposite examples. Imam Musa al-Kazim condemned Safwan Jammal's cooperation with Harun when it served Safwan's personal financial interest and included wishing for Harun's survival. By contrast, he encouraged 'Ali ibn Yaqtin to remain inside the Abbasid system while concealing his Shi'ism because his position could serve believers. Mutahhari's distinction is between being used by the ruling system and using a position to serve religious and social purposes.

title: Ch6 S2 — The example of Prophet Yusuf
text: Imam al-Rida is reported to have defended his position by comparing it with Prophet Yusuf's acceptance of administrative authority under the Egyptian ruler. Yusuf sought responsibility over the storehouses in order to use the position for a beneficial purpose; Imam al-Rida contrasted that voluntary request with his own forced acceptance. The example supports the principle that cooperation is evaluated partly by purpose and circumstances.

title: Ch6 S2 — Wilayat al-ja'ir and conditional cooperation
text: Mutahhari connects the discussion to the jurisprudential concept of undertaking a position under an unjust ruler. Although such cooperation is ordinarily prohibited, he explains that it can become permissible, recommended, or obligatory when the position is genuinely necessary to enjoin good, prevent evil, reduce oppression, or serve the Muslim community. The determining issue is the purpose and effect of the cooperation.

title: Ch6 S2 — The practical result of Imam al-Rida's appointment
text: Mutahhari argues that the crown-prince episode did not accomplish Ma'mun's presumed purpose of making Imam al-Rida a normal participant in government. Instead, the Imam retained his independence, his qualifications became more publicly visible, and the Ahl al-Bayt's standing was strengthened. The chapter therefore uses the episode to illustrate how the same outward act—holding a government position—can have different meanings depending on who controls its purpose.
